slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 10, use 10.2.1 Traversing Arrays Safely as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. Use a range-based loop when every element should be processed and the array object is still known. std::size(array) can obtain the extent without duplicating a numeric constant. Hard-coding a second size in a loop makes later edits fragile: the declaration can change while traversal still assumes the old count. When a raw array is passed to many ordinary function parameters, it decays to a pointer and its extent is no longer carried by that parameter. A declaration that visually resembles int values[4] in such a parameter does not enforce a four-element argument. Prefer an array reference, a standard container, or a span with a clear lifetime and extent contract as your interfaces become more advanced. slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 10, use 10.2.2 Processing Multidimensional Arrays as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. A declaration such as int grid[2][3] is an array of two arrays, each containing three integers. Traverse rows and columns within their respective bounds. The nested structure matters to the type system; it is not interchangeable with every pointer-to-pointer representation. For large numerical data, a flat vector with an explicit indexing function can make dimensions and storage ownership easier to manage. The row-major mapping row * columns + column must still be protected against invalid dimensions and arithmetic overflow. At this stage, use tiny fixed arrays to understand the relationship between shape and indexing before generalizing the representation. keyPoints: Out-of-bounds access is not defined to return zero, throw an exception, or crash immediately.

slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 10, use 10.3.1 Recognizing Out-of-Bounds Access as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. Out-of-bounds access is not defined to return zero, throw an exception, or crash immediately. It can read unrelated data, overwrite another object, or appear harmless until an optimized build changes the layout. A program that prints the expected result after an invalid access is still defective. Use bounds-aware interfaces, tests at zero and at the final valid index, compiler diagnostics, and sanitizers as complementary defenses. Do not create a test whose expected behavior depends on reading just past the end. Instead, test the validation path that rejects the invalid index before access. The contract is what must be verified, not an accidental symptom of violating it.
